arXiv:2611.17504v1 [eess.SY] 12 Nov 2026

Learning monotone game-theoretic linear MPC

Alberto Bemporad Affiliation: IMT School for Advanced Studies Lucca, Italy Email: alberto.bemporad@imtlucca.it    Tatiana Tatarenko Affiliation: Technische Universität Darmstadt, Germany Email: tatiana.tatarenko@tu-darmstadt.de
Abstract

We propose a method to learn a game-theoretic model predictive control (GT-MPC) law by imitation from input and output data of a running multi-agent system. By interpreting the recorded inputs as the first moves of the equilibria of a game played by the agents, we learn the GT-MPC weights under hard input constraints and soft output constraints, without requiring the agents to reveal their objectives. We also impose that the resulting generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) problem is strongly monotone, which ensures the existence and uniqueness of the equilibrium and, hence, that the learned GT-MPC law is well defined and can be evaluated efficiently online by variational GNE-seeking algorithms for linear-quadratic games. Moreover, strong monotonicity implies that the equilibrium is almost everywhere differentiable with respect to the references and the weights, which enables automatic differentiation for gradient-based optimization. In addition, we promote closed-loop stability of the unconstrained equilibrium feedback by incorporating a penalty that involves a jointly learned quadratic Lyapunov function. Learning a GT-MPC formulation enables us to explain the agents’ objectives, reproduce their behavior in simulation in new scenarios, optimize their set-points, design mechanisms, and enforce additional constraints. A numerical example illustrates the approach.

Keywords: Game-theoretic model predictive control, monotone games, inverse games, imitation learning, bilevel optimization

1 Introduction

In game-theoretic model predictive control (GT-MPC), several agents act on a common dynamical system, each optimizing a personal objective that depends on the other agents’ moves under local and shared constraints, and applying the first move of the resulting generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) at every time step [26, 18, 19, 8, 17, 13]. Each GT-MPC problem is a finite-horizon dynamic game; see [16, 21, 23] for solution algorithms and multi-vehicle applications. Modeling the agents’ costs is often difficult: the agents may be unwilling to disclose their objectives and strategies for privacy reasons, and in many applications the plant is even operated without explicit objectives to minimize, e.g., by standard decentralized control loops or even manually. A natural goal is then to learn, from the observed actions only, a GT-MPC law that reproduces them, so that the agents do not have to reveal their strategies, and that adds the main benefit of MPC, namely, handling input and output constraints. Moreover, once a game representation of agents’ behavior is available, it can be used for higher-level tasks, such as optimization of the set-point signals that enter the game at each step. It also allows reproducing the agents’ behavior in closed-loop simulation, e.g., on a digital twin of the plant, to evaluate what-if scenarios that have not been observed yet.

In this paper we reach this goal by imitation: we learn a game whose equilibria, given reference signals and estimated states, reproduce the agents’ actions. We restrict our attention to strongly monotone linear-quadratic (LQ) games. Roughly speaking, monotonicity plays for games the role that convexity plays for optimization: if the joint feasible set is nonempty, closed, and convex, a strongly monotone game has a unique variational GNE for every value of the parameter (here, the state estimate, reference, and previous input) [15]. So the learned control law is well defined and, as LQ-GNE problems can be solved efficiently [3, 7, 5], easily computable. Moreover, the variational GNE of a strongly monotone LQ game is a path-differentiable function of the parameters, whose derivatives can be computed by automatic differentiation [10], which makes gradient-based learning and equilibrium design well founded.

Unlike [9] and [1], who fit the agents’ objectives by minimizing the residuals of the variational inequality and of the KKT conditions at observed equilibria, respectively, we impose strong monotonicity of the learned game by construction, as also done in [22] through an LMI. Moreover, in [9, 1, 22] the number of unknowns grows linearly with the number of samples, as the dual variables of each sample are optimized. Finally, in our setting only the first move of each equilibrium is observed, not the entire sequence of planned moves that the methods in [9, 1, 22] would require to fit a GT-MPC formulation. Learning was also combined with GT-MPC in [20] for two autonomous vehicles: the GNEs of a known constrained dynamic game are computed offline from random initial conditions, and a neural network trained to predict their reward outcome is used as the terminal cost of each agent’s MPC problem. Here, instead, we learn the unknown costs from closed-loop data, do not assume decoupled dynamics, and solve the learned LQ game online.

We define a class of GT-MPC problems with soft shared output constraints based on a linear state-space model realization learned from the available input / output data. Then, we learn agent-specific weights and slack penalties by a bilevel problem whose inner problems are the LQ-GNE problems of the game at each datapoint, in which strong monotonicity holds by construction and closed-loop stability of the unconstrained Nash equilibrium feedback is enforced by a penalty involving a jointly learned quadratic Lyapunov function, so that the problem can be solved by L-BFGS-B. We illustrate in a numerical example that we can reconstruct an underlying game played by the agents very precisely and shape closed-loop behavior by reference optimization.

Section 2 presents the problem setting, Section 3 recalls monotone LQ games, Section 3.1 characterizes the monotonicity of the GT-MPC game, Section 3.2 presents the bilevel learning problem and its solution algorithm, Section 3.3 closed-loop stability, Section 4 a numerical example, and Section 5 conclusions. The code is available at https://github.com/bemporad/gtmpc_learn.

3 Learning monotone GT-MPC games

In a parametric LQ game with constant agents’ Hessian matrices and affine dependence on the parameter pp in the linear cost terms, agent ii minimizes over zi=(xi,ϵi)z_{i}=(x_{i},\epsilon_{i}) the cost

Ji​(z,p)=12​zi⊤​A¯i​i​zi+∑j≠izi⊤​A¯i​j​zj+q¯i​(p)⊤​zi+(terms not depending on ​zi)J_{i}(z;p)=\tfrac{1}{2}z_{i}^{\top}\bar{A}_{ii}z_{i}+\sum_{j\neq i}z_{i}^{\top}\bar{A}_{ij}z_{j}+\bar{q}_{i}(p)^{\top}z_{i}+(\text{terms not depending on }z_{i}) (4)

where z=(x,ϵ)z=(x,\epsilon), A¯i​i\bar{A}_{ii} is symmetric, and q¯i​(p)\bar{q}_{i}(p) is affine in pp. Agent ii’s problem is convex when A¯i​i⪰0\bar{A}_{ii}\succeq 0. The pseudogradient F⁡(z,p)F(z;p) collects the agents’ gradients ∇ziJi​(z,p)\nabla_{z_{i}}J_{i}(z;p) with respect to their own decision variables, in the same ordering as zz, so that F​(z,p)=A¯​z+q¯​(p)F(z;p)=\bar{A}z+\bar{q}(p), with A¯=[A¯i​j]∈ℝnz×nz\bar{A}=[\bar{A}_{ij}]\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{z}\times n_{z}} and q¯\bar{q} collecting the vectors q¯i\bar{q}_{i}, where nz=nu​Tu+Nn_{z}=n_{u}T_{u}+N. The game is monotone with constant μ≥0\mu\geq 0 [15, 24] if (F⁡(z,p)−F⁡(z′,p))⊤​(z−z′)≥μ​‖z−z′‖22(F(z;p)-F(z^{\prime};p))^{\top}(z-z^{\prime})\geq\mu\|z-z^{\prime}\|_{2}^{2} for all z,z′z,z^{\prime}, which here is the same as

sym⁡(A¯)⪰μ​Inz.\sym(\bar{A})\succeq\mu I_{n_{z}}. (5)

When μ>0\mu>0 the game is strongly monotone. With a shared constraint z∈𝒵⁡(p)z\in\mathcal{Z}(p), where 𝒵⁡(p)\mathcal{Z}(p) is nonempty, closed, and convex, the variational GNEs are the solutions of the variational inequality defined by F⁡(⋅,p)F(\cdot;p) on 𝒵⁡(p)\mathcal{Z}(p) [14]. Since FF is continuous and strongly monotone, this variational inequality has a unique solution [15], so the game has a unique variational GNE.

The pseudogradient of the GT-MPC game is F⁡(z,p)=(A​x+q⁡(p),qϵ+2​Qϵ​ϵ)F(z;p)=\bigl(Ax+q(p),\,q_{\epsilon}+2Q_{\epsilon}\epsilon\bigr), with A=[Ai​j]∈ℝnu​Tu×nu​TuA=[A_{ij}]\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{u}T_{u}\times n_{u}T_{u}}, q=(q1,…,qN)q=(q_{1},\ldots,q_{N}), qϵ=(qϵ,1,…,qϵ,N)q_{\epsilon}=(q_{\epsilon,1},\ldots,q_{\epsilon,N}) and Qϵ=diag⁡(Qϵ,1,…,Qϵ,N)Q_{\epsilon}=\mathrm{diag}(Q_{\epsilon,1},\ldots,Q_{\epsilon,N}), whose Jacobian with respect to zz is A¯=blkdiag⁡(A,2​Qϵ)\bar{A}=\blkdiag(A,2Q_{\epsilon}), and q¯​(p)=(q⁡(p),qϵ)\bar{q}(p)=(q(p),q_{\epsilon}). So, by (5), the game is strongly monotone in zz, with constant μ>0\mu>0, if and only if

sym⁡(A)⪰μ​Inu​TuQϵ,i≥μ2,i=1,…,N.\sym(A)\succeq\mu I_{n_{u}T_{u}}\qquad Q_{\epsilon,i}\geq\frac{\mu}{2},\quad i=1,\ldots,N. (7)

For a fixed model, the first condition is an LMI in (Qy,i,QΔ​u,i)i=1N(Q_{y,i},Q_{\Delta u,i})_{i=1}^{N}, and the second one is a simple bound on each quadratic slack penalty.

Proposition 1.

Suppose that (7) holds with μ>0\mu>0, that uk−1∈𝒰u_{k-1}\in\mathcal{U}, and that the bounds on the increments contain 00. Then, for every pp, the GT-MPC game has a unique variational GNE z⋆​(p)=(x⋆​(p),ϵ⋆​(p))z^{\star}(p)=(x^{\star}(p),\epsilon^{\star}(p)).

Proof.

The shared feasible set is closed and convex, and it is nonempty, since x=0x=0 with large enough slacks is feasible. By (7), F⁡(⋅,p)F(\cdot;p) is continuous and strongly monotone with constant μ\mu on this set, so the variational inequality that it defines on the set has a unique solution [15], which is the unique variational GNE. ∎

3.2 Learning problem

Our goal now is to set up a learning problem that identifies all the weights in (2) such that the resulting game is strongly monotone, i.e., satisfies (7). Since the pseudogradient matrix of the GT-MPC game is constrained to the structure (6), we cannot directly exploit the form A=W⊤​W+D−D⊤+μ​Inu​TuA=W^{\top}W+D-D^{\top}+\mu I_{n_{u}T_{u}} that characterizes every strongly monotone LQ game, as was recently shown in [6, Lemma 4.4], where WW is upper triangular and DD is block strictly upper triangular. Instead, let us parametrize the agent-specific weights with variables Cy,i∈ℝny×nyC_{y,i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{y}\times n_{y}}, Ci∈ℝni×niC_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{i}\times n_{i}}, and Si∈ℝni×(nu−ni)S_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{i}\times(n_{u}-n_{i})}, i=1,…,Ni=1,\ldots,N, where Qy,i=Cy,i⊤​Cy,iQ_{y,i}=C_{y,i}^{\top}C_{y,i}, SiS_{i} are the cross weights on input increments, and the own weights are

QΔ​u,ii​i=Ci⊤​Ci+(η+c⁡(θ))​Inic⁡(θ)=12​[μ−λmin​(sym⁡(A~​(θ)))]+Q^{ii}_{\Delta u,i}=C_{i}^{\top}C_{i}+\bigl(\eta+c(\theta)\bigr)I_{n_{i}}\qquad c(\theta)=\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl[\mu-\lambda_{\min}\bigl(\sym(\tilde{A}(\theta))\bigr)\bigr]_{+} (8)

where η>0\eta>0 is small and fixed, while A~​(θ)\tilde{A}(\theta) is the pseudogradient matrix (6) obtained with c⁡(θ)=0c(\theta)=0. By (6), adding c​InicI_{n_{i}} to each QΔ​u,ii​iQ^{ii}_{\Delta u,i} provides λmin​(sym⁡(A⁡(θ)))≥μ\lambda_{\min}(\sym(A(\theta)))\geq\mu for every θ\theta. The remaining block E¯−i​QΔ​u,i​E¯−i⊤\bar{E}_{-i}Q_{\Delta u,i}\bar{E}_{-i}^{\top} does not affect the game; after learning we set it to Si⊤​(QΔ​u,ii​i)−1​SiS_{i}^{\top}(Q^{ii}_{\Delta u,i})^{-1}S_{i}, the smallest block for which QΔ​u,i⪰0Q_{\Delta u,i}\succeq 0. The slack penalties qϵ,iq_{\epsilon,i} and Qϵ,iQ_{\epsilon,i} are scalars and are kept directly as optimization variables. Then, we learn the agent-specific weights and the slack penalties by solving

minθ1N​K​∑k=1K‖u¯k​(θ)−uk‖22+ρ2​∑i=1N(‖Qy,i‖F2+‖QΔ​u,ii​i‖F2+2​‖Si‖F2)subject toqϵ,i≥0,Qϵ,i≥μ2,i=1,…,N\begin{array}[]{ll}\mbox{min}_{\theta}&\displaystyle\frac{1}{NK}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\bigl\|\bar{u}_{k}(\theta)-u_{k}\bigr\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{\rho}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\bigl(\|Q_{y,i}\|_{F}^{2}+\|Q^{ii}_{\Delta u,i}\|_{F}^{2}+2\|S_{i}\|_{F}^{2}\bigr)\\[2.0pt] \mbox{subject to}&q_{\epsilon,i}\geq 0,\quad Q_{\epsilon,i}\geq\dfrac{\mu}{2},\quad i=1,\ldots,N\end{array} (9)

where θ=(Cy,i,Ci,Si,qϵ,i,Qϵ,i)i=1N\theta=(C_{y,i},C_{i},S_{i},q_{\epsilon,i},Q_{\epsilon,i})_{i=1}^{N} is the vector that collects all the learnable parameters of the game, uku_{k} is the measured input at sample step kk, and u¯k​(θ)=uk−1+Ef​x⋆​(pk,θ)\bar{u}_{k}(\theta)=u_{k-1}+E_{\mathrm{f}}\,x^{\star}(p_{k};\theta) is the first move of the variational GNE

z⋆​(pk,θ)=(x⋆​(pk,θ),ϵ⋆​(pk,θ))z^{\star}(p_{k};\theta)=(x^{\star}(p_{k};\theta),\epsilon^{\star}(p_{k};\theta))

of the game (2) with the weights θ\theta at the parameter pkp_{k}. The scalar ρ>0\rho>0 weights the regularization of the weights Qy,iQ_{y,i}, QΔ​u,ii​iQ^{ii}_{\Delta u,i}, and SiS_{i}.

Due to the GNE terms u¯k​(θ)\bar{u}_{k}(\theta), the optimization problem in (9) is a bilevel problem, whose lower-level problems are the GNE problems of the game at the parameters pkp_{k}. By Proposition 1, u¯k​(θ)\bar{u}_{k}(\theta) is uniquely defined for all kk and admissible θ\theta, as the measured inputs satisfy the input constraints. For compactness of notation, in (9) we drop the superscript jj and number all the sample steps of all experiments consecutively as k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K. We describe below how we solve this bound-constrained bilevel nonlinear least-squares problem with L-BFGS-B [12], including the initial guess and the computation of the GNEs and of their derivatives with respect to θ\theta.

Initialization.

We initialize the components of θ\theta as

Cy,i=\displaystyle C_{y,i}= s​InyCi=μ+δ2−η​IniSi=0qϵ,i=qϵ0Qϵ,i=Qϵ0\displaystyle\sqrt{s}\,I_{n_{y}}\quad C_{i}=\sqrt{\tfrac{\mu+\delta}{2}-\eta}\,I_{n_{i}}\quad S_{i}=0\quad q_{\epsilon,i}=q^{0}_{\epsilon}\quad Q_{\epsilon,i}=Q^{0}_{\epsilon}
i=1,…,N\displaystyle i=1,\ldots,N

where s≥0s\geq 0 is a scale factor, δ>0\delta>0 is small, η≤(μ+δ)/2\eta\leq(\mu+\delta)/2, qϵ0>0q^{0}_{\epsilon}>0, and Qϵ0≥μ/2Q^{0}_{\epsilon}\geq\mu/2. Then (6) gives the symmetric matrix A~​(θ)=2​s​Γ¯⊤​Γ¯+(μ+δ)​Inu​Tu⪰(μ+δ)​Inu​Tu\tilde{A}(\theta)=2s\bar{\Gamma}^{\top}\bar{\Gamma}+(\mu+\delta)I_{n_{u}T_{u}}\succeq(\mu+\delta)I_{n_{u}T_{u}} for every s≥0s\geq 0, where Γ¯=[Γ1⋯ΓN]\bar{\Gamma}=[\Gamma_{1}\ \cdots\ \Gamma_{N}], so that c⁡(θ)=0c(\theta)=0 at the initial point. With the slack penalties fixed to qϵ0q^{0}_{\epsilon} and Qϵ0Q^{0}_{\epsilon}, we choose ss by minimizing the imitation loss, i.e., the first term of the objective in (9), over a logarithmic grid of values of ss, which requires solving KK LQ-GNE problems for each grid value.

Computing the GNEs and their derivatives.

As L-BFGS-B is a gradient-based method, we need to differentiate the LQ-GNEs z⋆​(pk,θ)z^{\star}(p_{k};\theta) with respect to θ\theta efficiently. Recall that the pseudogradient of the game is A¯​(θ)​z+q¯​(p)\bar{A}(\theta)z+\bar{q}(p), with A¯​(θ)=blkdiag⁡(A⁡(θ),2​Qϵ)\bar{A}(\theta)=\blkdiag(A(\theta),2Q_{\epsilon}) and q¯​(p)=(q⁡(p),qϵ)\bar{q}(p)=(q(p),q_{\epsilon}), and let G​z≤b⁡(pk)Gz\leq b(p_{k}) collect the shared constraints of (2), where bb also depends on uk−1u_{k-1}. As by strong monotonicity (5) matrix A¯​(θ)\bar{A}(\theta) is invertible, by [7, Lemma 5.1] the variational GNE is zk⋆=z0,k−A¯−1​G⊤​λk⋆z^{\star}_{k}=z_{0,k}-\bar{A}^{-1}G^{\top}\lambda^{\star}_{k}, z0,k=−A¯−1​q¯​(pk)z_{0,k}=-\bar{A}^{-1}\bar{q}(p_{k}), where λk⋆\lambda^{\star}_{k} solves the QP

minλ​λ⊤​sym⁡(H)​λ+q0,k⊤​λs.t.​H​λ+q0,k≥0,λ≥0\mbox{min}_{\lambda}\ \lambda^{\top}\sym(H)\lambda+q_{0,k}^{\top}\lambda\quad\mbox{s.t.}\ H\lambda+q_{0,k}\geq 0,\ \lambda\geq 0 (10)

with H=G​A¯−1​G⊤H=G\bar{A}^{-1}G^{\top} and q0,k=b⁡(pk)−G​z0,kq_{0,k}=b(p_{k})-Gz_{0,k}. Although u¯k​(θ)\bar{u}_{k}(\theta) and its derivatives could be obtained directly by solving (10) with a differentiable QP solver [2, 25], we take a more efficient approach here. Let θj\theta^{j} be the value of the parameters at the jj-th iteration of the learning algorithm. We compute zk⋆​(θj)z^{\star}_{k}(\theta^{j}) by a tailored LQ-GNE solver (such as DR-DAQP [3]) and identify the set 𝒜k​(θj)\mathcal{A}_{k}(\theta^{j}) of constraints with positive multipliers (we drop the dependence on θj\theta^{j} from now on for simplicity of notation). Then, we write zk⋆=z0,k−A¯−1​G𝒜k⊤​λ𝒜kz^{\star}_{k}=z_{0,k}-\bar{A}^{-1}G_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}^{\top}\lambda_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}, where G𝒜k​A¯−1​G𝒜k⊤​λ𝒜k=G𝒜k​z0,k−b𝒜k​(pk)G_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}\bar{A}^{-1}G_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}^{\top}\lambda_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}=G_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}z_{0,k}-b_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}(p_{k}) are the rows of H​λ+q0,k=0H\lambda+q_{0,k}=0 of the active constraints. For a fixed active set, this is a linear system H𝒜k​(θ)​λ𝒜k=hk​(θ)H_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}(\theta)\lambda_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}=h_{k}(\theta), with H𝒜k=G𝒜k​A¯−1​G𝒜k⊤H_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}=G_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}\bar{A}^{-1}G_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}^{\top} and hk=G𝒜k​z0,k−b𝒜k​(pk)h_{k}=G_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}z_{0,k}-b_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}(p_{k}), whose coefficients depend smoothly on θ\theta through A¯​(θ)\bar{A}(\theta) and q¯​(pk)\bar{q}(p_{k}). If the rows of G𝒜kG_{\mathcal{A}_{k}} are linearly independent, the multipliers λ𝒜k\lambda_{\mathcal{A}_{k}} are positive, and the inactive constraints are strictly satisfied, the active set does not change for small perturbations of θ\theta. Then λ𝒜k​(θ)\lambda_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}(\theta), zk⋆​(θ)z^{\star}_{k}(\theta), and hence u¯k​(θ)\bar{u}_{k}(\theta) are smooth functions of θ\theta around θj\theta^{j}, with d​λ𝒜k=H𝒜k−1​(d​hk−d​H𝒜k​λ𝒜k)\mathrm{d}\lambda_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}=H_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}^{-1}(\mathrm{d}h_{k}-\mathrm{d}H_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}\lambda_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}), obtained by differentiating H𝒜k​λ𝒜k=hkH_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}\lambda_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}=h_{k}, and hence d​zk⋆=d​z0,k−d⁡(A¯−1)​G𝒜k⊤​λ𝒜k−A¯−1​G𝒜k⊤​d​λ𝒜k\mathrm{d}z^{\star}_{k}=\mathrm{d}z_{0,k}-\mathrm{d}(\bar{A}^{-1})\,G_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}^{\top}\lambda_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}-\bar{A}^{-1}G_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}^{\top}\mathrm{d}\lambda_{\mathcal{A}_{k}}. In our numerical experiments, we implement the map from θ\theta to the imitation loss through these linear systems in JAX [11].

3.3 Closed-loop stability enforcement

Strong monotonicity guarantees that the GT-MPC law is well defined, but not that the closed loop is asymptotically stable. Without constraints, the variational GNE is x⋆​(p)=−A​(θ)−1​q​(p)x^{\star}(p)=-A(\theta)^{-1}q(p), which is linear in p=(ξ^k,uk−1,rk)p=(\hat{\xi}_{k},u_{k-1},r_{k}), so that the vector of first input increments of all agents is Kξ​(θ)​ξ^k+Ku​(θ)​uk−1+Kr​(θ)​rkK_{\xi}(\theta)\hat{\xi}_{k}+K_{u}(\theta)u_{k-1}+K_{r}(\theta)r_{k}. In closed loop with the identified model and ξ^k=ξk\hat{\xi}_{k}=\xi_{k}, the state ζk=(ξk,uk−1)\zeta_{k}=(\xi_{k},u_{k-1}) evolves as ζk+1=M⁡(θ)​ζk+Mr​(θ)​rk\zeta_{k+1}=M(\theta)\zeta_{k}+M_{r}(\theta)r_{k}, for some matrix Mr​(θ)M_{r}(\theta), where M⁡(θ)=[𝒜+ℬ​Kξ​(θ)ℬ​(I+Ku​(θ))Kξ​(θ)I+Ku​(θ)]M(\theta)=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}{\mathcal{A}}+{\mathcal{B}}K_{\xi}(\theta)&{\mathcal{B}}\bigl(I+K_{u}(\theta)\bigr)\\ K_{\xi}(\theta)&I+K_{u}(\theta)\end{smallmatrix}\right]. Under the assumption that the observed multi-agent system generating the training data is asymptotically stable, we can enforce asymptotic stability of the unconstrained closed loop a priori by adding to the objective of (9) the following penalty

ρs​[‖L​M​(θ)​L−1‖22−γ2]+2\rho_{s}\bigl[\|LM(\theta)L^{-1}\|_{2}^{2}-\gamma^{2}\bigr]_{+}^{2} (11)

where ρs>0\rho_{s}>0 weights the penalty relative to the imitation loss, γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1) is a desired contraction rate, and the matrix L∈ℝ(n+nu)×(n+nu)L\in\mathbb{R}^{(n+n_{u})\times(n+n_{u})}, upper triangular with positive diagonal, is learned together with θ\theta. Since ‖L​M​L−1‖2<1\|LML^{-1}\|_{2}<1 is equivalent to M⊤​P​M≺PM^{\top}PM\prec P with P=L⊤​LP=L^{\top}L, a value of ‖L​M​(θ)​L−1‖2\|LM(\theta)L^{-1}\|_{2} below 11 certifies the quadratic Lyapunov function ζ⊤​P​ζ\zeta^{\top}P\zeta of the unconstrained closed loop. Conversely, by [4, Lemma 1] applied to M/γM/\gamma, for every matrix MM with spectral radius smaller than γ\gamma there exists such an LL, given by the Cholesky factor of the solution of a Lyapunov equation, for which ‖L​M​L−1‖2<γ\|LML^{-1}\|_{2}<\gamma, so the penalty can be zeroed for every game whose closed-loop matrix M⁡(θ)M(\theta) has spectral radius smaller than γ\gamma. As (11) is a penalty, we check that ‖L​M​(θ)​L−1‖2<1\|LM(\theta)L^{-1}\|_{2}<1 at the solution and, otherwise, increase ρs\rho_{s} and solve the problem again starting from the current solution. By the separation principle, stability of M⁡(θ)M(\theta) also implies stability of the nominal closed loop with the Kalman filter when constraints are not active, although it does not guarantee global closed-loop stability under constraints, nor robustness to the mismatch between the identified model and the actual process.

4 Numerical example

Generating system.

We consider a randomly generated open-loop stable process with nu=3n_{u}=3 inputs, ny=3n_{y}=3 outputs, n=4n=4 states, and N=3N=3 agents, each commanding one input. The constraints are |ui|≤0.15|u_{i}|\leq 0.15, |Δ​ui|≤0.1|\Delta u_{i}|\leq 0.1, and we want to enforce |yi|≤ymax=3|y_{i}|\leq y_{\textrm{max}}=3. The agents operate the process by playing a GT-MPC game of the form (2) with T=Tc=10T=T_{c}=10, Tu=4T_{u}=4, the true model and state, the soft output constraints |yi|≤3|y_{i}|\leq 3 with the slack penalties qϵ,i=0.003q_{\epsilon,i}=0.003 and Qϵ,i=0.5Q_{\epsilon,i}=0.5, and the weights Qy,1=10−4​diag​(1,0.6,0.1)Q_{y,1}=10^{-4}\mathrm{diag}(1,0.6,0.1), Qy,2=10−4​diag​(0.1,1,0.6)Q_{y,2}=10^{-4}\mathrm{diag}(0.1,1,0.6), Qy,3=10−4​diag​(0.6,0.1,1)Q_{y,3}=10^{-4}\mathrm{diag}(0.6,0.1,1), and QΔ​u,i=wi​ei​ei⊤Q_{\Delta u,i}=w_{i}e_{i}e_{i}^{\top}, where eie_{i} is the iith column of I3I_{3} and (w1,w2,w3)=(0.05,0.1,0.2)(w_{1},w_{2},w_{3})=(0.05,0.1,0.2). The pseudogradient matrix AA of this game is not symmetric, ‖A−A⊤‖F/‖A‖F=0.30\|A-A^{\top}\|_{F}/\|A\|_{F}=0.30, so the game is not a potential game that can be represented by a single centralized MPC cost. It is also strongly monotone, with λmin​(sym⁡(A))=0.106\lambda_{\min}(\sym(A))=0.106. All three inputs and outputs are dynamically coupled by the system dynamics.

Data collection.

We record ne=7n_{\mathrm{e}}=7 experiments of 200200 steps in which the agents operate according to the underlying (unknown) GT-MPC strategy. Each experiment starts from the equilibrium of a reference uniformly distributed in [−1.5,1.5]3[-1.5,1.5]^{3}, a range in which the corresponding equilibrium input always satisfies the input constraints, and the references of all the agents are piecewise constant, with new values uniformly distributed in [−5,5]3[-5,5]^{3} every 1515 steps. The output noise is uniformly distributed in [−0.05,0.05][-0.05,0.05].

Learning.

Using jax-sysid, we first identify a model with n=4n=4 states from these closed-loop data in 2.32.3 s22 2 All the reported CPU times were obtained on an Apple M5 Max machine in Python 3.11.15. . On 33 further experiments generated in the same way, the open-loop simulation of the identified model, from the initial states estimated by jax-sysid, achieves best fit rates 100​(1−‖yl−y^l‖2/‖yl−y¯l‖2)100\bigl(1-\|y_{l}-\hat{y}_{l}\|_{2}/\|y_{l}-\bar{y}_{l}\|_{2}\bigr) of 98.7%98.7\%, 98.6%98.6\%, and 98.7%98.7\% on the outputs l=1,2,3l=1,2,3, where yly_{l} collects the measured values of output ll, y^l\hat{y}_{l} the simulated ones, and y¯l\bar{y}_{l} is the mean of yly_{l}.

For the GT-MPC structure to learn, we use T=Tc=10T=T_{c}=10, μ=0.1\mu=0.1, ρ=10−5\rho=10^{-5}, η=10−3\eta=10^{-3}, and different values of TuT_{u} between 1 and TT. We initialize the bilevel problem with qϵ0=10−3q^{0}_{\epsilon}=10^{-3}, Qϵ0=0.1Q^{0}_{\epsilon}=0.1, and δ=0.01\delta=0.01, searching ss over the grid log10⁡s∈{−10,−9.5,…,−2}\log_{10}s\in\{-10,-9.5,\ldots,-2\} for initializing the solution of (9), which we solve by the L-BFGS-B solver of SciPy with the stability penalty (11), γ=0.9\gamma=0.9, and ρs=10\rho_{s}=10. The Kalman filter uses the process noise covariance 10−6​I410^{-6}I_{4}, the measurement noise covariance 0.0523​I3\frac{0.05^{2}}{3}I_{3}, and the initial covariance 10−4​I410^{-4}I_{4}.

Controller.

At each time step kk, the GT-MPC law estimates ξ^k\hat{\xi}_{k} by a Kalman filter based on the identified model, sets pk=(ξ^k,uk−1,rk)p_{k}=(\hat{\xi}_{k},u_{k-1},r_{k}), and computes the variational GNE of (2), which exists and is unique by Proposition 1, by the DR-DAQP solver [3] through the nashopt package [5].

Results.

We validate the controllers on 1010 runs of 8080 steps, each with a set-point change from r0r^{0} to r1r^{1}, starting from the equilibrium of r0r^{0}. Each component of r1r^{1} is uniformly distributed in [−2.7,2.7][-2.7,2.7], and r0=r1−sign⁡(r1)∘dr^{0}=r^{1}-\mathrm{sign}(r^{1})\circ d, with dd uniformly distributed in [0,3]3[0,3]^{3}. The Kalman filter of the GT-MPC law starts from the equilibrium state of the identified model for r0r^{0}. Table 1 reports, for different values of TuT_{u}, the training time, the monotonicity constant λmin​(sym⁡(A⁡(θ)))\lambda_{\min}(\sym(A(\theta))) of the learned game, and the closed-loop imitation errors

RMSu=\displaystyle\textrm{RMS}_{u}= (∑j=110∑k=079‖ukj−ua,kj‖22∑j=110∑k=079‖ua,kj‖22)1/2\displaystyle\biggl(\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{10}\sum_{k=0}^{79}\|u^{j}_{k}-u^{j}_{\mathrm{a},k}\|_{2}^{2}}{\sum_{j=1}^{10}\sum_{k=0}^{79}\|u^{j}_{\mathrm{a},k}\|_{2}^{2}}\biggr)^{1/2}
RMSy=\displaystyle\textrm{RMS}_{y}= (∑j=110∑k=079‖ykj−ya,kj‖22∑j=110∑k=079‖ya,kj‖22)1/2\displaystyle\biggl(\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{10}\sum_{k=0}^{79}\|y^{j}_{k}-y^{j}_{\mathrm{a},k}\|_{2}^{2}}{\sum_{j=1}^{10}\sum_{k=0}^{79}\|y^{j}_{\mathrm{a},k}\|_{2}^{2}}\biggr)^{1/2}

where (ykj,ukj)(y^{j}_{k},u^{j}_{k}) and (ya,kj,ua,kj)(y^{j}_{\mathrm{a},k},u^{j}_{\mathrm{a},k}) are the measured outputs and the inputs of the closed loops with the GT-MPC law and with the agents in run jj. The average CPU time per step taken by the solver to evaluate the GT-MPC action ranges between 2121 and 9696 μ\mus depending on the control horizon TuT_{u}. With closed-loop stability enforced, the GT-MPC law learned by (9) imitates the agents with imitation errors below 0.0710.071 for all TuT_{u}, and the smallest for Tu=4T_{u}=4, which is the control horizon indeed used by the agents generating the training data.

Figure 1 shows a run of the GT-MPC law learned by (9) with Tu=4T_{u}=4. The GT-MPC law produces closed-loop trajectories that are almost indistinguishable from those of the agents. As shown in Table 1 (left), for Tu=4T_{u}=4 the learned weights are close to those of the agents up to a common scale factor α=0.89\alpha=0.89, which leaves the GNEs unchanged, and the off-diagonal entries of Qy,iQ_{y,i} and the cross weights SiS_{i} are small, below 1.6⋅10−61.6\cdot 10^{-6} and 2.8⋅10−32.8\cdot 10^{-3} in magnitude, respectively. With the stability penalty, the unconstrained closed loops are asymptotically stable for all TuT_{u} (spectral radius between 0.720.72 and 0.850.85).

4.1 Set-point optimization

The learned game can be used for higher-level tasks without requiring the agents to reveal their objectives. As an example, a reference generator placed on top of the agents, who keep playing their own GT-MPC game, sends them at each step kk the reference

rk=arg​minr⁡(y^1​(r)−r1,kdes)2+ω​∑l=23(y^l​(r)−rl,kdes)2+σ​‖r−rkdes‖22r_{k}=\argmin_{r}\ \bigl(\hat{y}_{1}(r)-r^{\mathrm{des}}_{1,k}\bigr)^{2}+\omega\sum_{l=2}^{3}\bigl(\hat{y}_{l}(r)-r^{\mathrm{des}}_{l,k}\bigr)^{2}+\sigma\|r-r^{\mathrm{des}}_{k}\|_{2}^{2} (12)

where rkdesr^{\mathrm{des}}_{k} is the reference of Figure 1 to track, y^​(r)=𝒞⁡(𝒜​ξ^k+ℬ​u¯k​(r))\hat{y}(r)=\mathcal{C}\bigl(\mathcal{A}\hat{\xi}_{k}+\mathcal{B}\bar{u}_{k}(r)\bigr) is the output predicted by the identified model when the agents apply the GT-MPC action u¯k​(r)\bar{u}_{k}(r) of the game learned with Tu=4T_{u}=4 at p=(ξ^k,uk−1,r)p=(\hat{\xi}_{k},u_{k-1},r), ω∈(0,1)\omega\in(0,1) reduces the importance of tracking y2y_{2} and y3y_{3}, and σ>0\sigma>0 prevents excessive deviations of rr from rkdesr^{\mathrm{des}}_{k}. We solve (12) by a Gauss-Newton method, using the derivatives of the GNE of Section 3.2. As shown in Figure 1 (green) for ω=0.02\omega=0.02 and σ=10−2\sigma=10^{-2}, the generator largely removes the dip and the bump of y1y_{1} caused by the coupling with the other loops (see red circles), at the price of slower transients of y2y_{2} and y3y_{3}.

5 Conclusions

We have proposed a method for learning strongly monotone GT-MPC laws from input/output data of multiple agents, and illustrated the use of the learned game for explaining the agents’ objectives and for optimizing the references given to the agents. Future research will address other higher-level uses of the learned game, such as mechanism design, and extensions to state-dependent weights and nonlinear systems.
